articleHeadline: Gonorrhea: influencer reveals a serious consequence due to an STI and how they ended up in surgery; find out
articleSummary: Gonorrhea, caused by Neisseria gonorrhoeae, affected Brazilian influencer Gabriel Madureira who disclosed infection six years ago, leading to urethral stricture (stenosis) that required urethroplasty and circumcision to remove calcified tissue and reconstruct the urethra. Postoperative recovery involved about 20–30 days with a catheter and a month of limited activity and no sexual relations. The article frames gonorrhea as a common sexually transmitted infection transmitted mainly through unprotected sex, with oral sex also possible. Symptoms differ by sex: roughly 90% of men are symptomatic (painful urination, penile discharge, testicular pain); about 80% of women are asymptomatic, with potential lower abdominal pain, yellow discharge, and dyspareunia. Diagnosis uses microscopy, culture, or DNA tests on vaginal or penile secretions; urine or saliva DNA tests are also available. Since 2023, Brazil’s SUS offers saliva testing in 82 laboratories. Treatment is antibiotic, typically injectable.

articleHeadline: Duque de Caxias prepares actions to combat Hansen's disease | Duque de Caxias | O Dia
articleSummary: Duque de Caxias launches actions for the State Day of Leprosy Combat (Aug 5) with skin-exam screenings, educational talks, and distribution of informational materials from Aug 3–7 to raise awareness of Hansen’s disease. Activities occur at UPH Campos Elíseos, Clínica da Família Imbariê, CMSDC Centro Municipal de Saúde, UPH Parque Equitativa, UPH Saracuruna, Hospital Municipal Duque/Policlínica, UPH Pilar, Clínica da Família Parque Fluminense, and UPH Xerém (Aug 7 11:00–12:00). Leprosy is caused by Mycobacterium leprae, an infectious, notifiable disease primarily affecting skin and peripheral nerves; transmission ceases once antibiotic treatment begins. Treatment lasts roughly six months to a year and is safe and effective, with care available at UPHs, CMSDC, and Hospital Municipal Duque. Early diagnosis and seeking health services are emphasized to curb spread.

articleHeadline: Climate Change is making malaria worse in parts of Africa while wiping it out in others, new study finds
articleSummary: As of 3 August 2026, a Nature study led by Colin J. Carlson and colleagues finds climate change is reshaping Africa’s malaria map: transmission worsens in cooler southern and East Africa, while hot West Africa and the Sahel edge toward parasite-elimination. Analyzing over 50,000 medical surveys from 1900–2016, the researchers project future changes through 2100, noting a continent-wide modest rise in malaria (about 1 extra case per 1,000 children aged 2–10) yet with regional contrasts. Malaria remains a major killer, with 2024 global cases at about 282 million and 610,000 deaths, 95% in Africa and 76% of African deaths in children under five. Temperature drives transmission: optimal around 25°C, dropping below 16°C or rising above 34°C reduces spread. South Africa (+17.78 per 1,000 by 2100) and Rwanda (+16.11) show biggest increases, while Niger (−23.62), Mali (−23.55), Mauritania (−23.50), and Burkina Faso (−20.71) show the largest declines; Ghana is projected to improve steadily, though climate change is a modest factor compared with vector control. A separate March 2026 report warns heat remains deadly even where malaria declines due to climate change.

articleHeadline: Togo: The fight against malaria is progressing in the Oti Region.
articleSummary: Malaria control in Togo's Oti district, part of the Savanes region near the Ghana and Burkina Faso border, shows progress with the distribution of 86,506 insecticide-treated bed nets to households, achieving 93.2% coverage. This effort is part of a national campaign to equip all households with at least one net for every two people. Malaria remains year-round in northern areas and intensifies during the rainy season when Anopheles mosquitoes multiply. ITNs provide a dual barrier—physical by shielding sleepers and chemical via the insecticide—reducing exposure and transmission. Regular use is linked to significant declines in malaria cases, especially among children under five and pregnant women. With coverage above 93%, health authorities have a solid foundation to continue reducing malaria in the Oti/Savanes region. Keywords: malaria, ITNs, Oti district, Savanes region, vector control, public health campaign.
